detail.readme:
AX

> [!WARNING] > AX and several of its features are in heavy development. We are actively > refining our core concepts, protocols, and specifications, and will likely > introduce major breaking changes prior to a stable release. **Declare an agentic task with workspaces and model specifications. AX sandboxes it, wires up its workspace, and helps running it at scale.** AX is a highly efficient, declarative orchestrator to run millions of autonomous agent workloads in a cluster. It runs on top of [Agent Substrate](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate) for sandboxed execution and is built to run millions of tasks per cluster. If you have used Kubernetes, `ax` will feel similar. ```yaml # task.yaml apiVersion: ax.io/v1alpha1 kind: Workspace metadata: name: golang spec: profile: # tasks that bind this workspace and omit spec.profile use it image: "ghcr.io/my-org/my-coding-agent@sha256:..." setup: git: - repo: https://github.com/golang/go.git ref: "my-fix" files: - path: "AGENTS.md" content: | - Run `go test` to ensure that tests are passing. - Do not modify the public API. --- apiVersion: ax.io/v1alpha1 kind: Task metadata: name: test spec: goal: text: "Fix what's broken please." workspace: name: golang debug: true # enables `ax ssh` ``` Then apply it, resume it, and look over the agent's shoulder: ```bash ax apply -f task.yaml ax resume task test ax describe task test ax ssh test -- ls -al /workspace ``` ## Why? Agents are a new kind of workload. They are neither stateless microservices nor run-to-completion batch jobs. They accumulate state, need strict isolation, call out to model APIs and tool servers, and can burn money in a loop if nobody is watching. AX gives you three small primitives that handle all of that declaratively: | You want to... | AX gives you | |---|---| | Run untrusted agent code in an isolated sandbox with CPU/memory limits | **`Task`** | | Pre-wire Git repos, MCP servers, and skill packages so every agent starts warm | **`Workspace`** | | Configure which LLM the platform itself uses, with credentials from a Kubernetes secret | **`Model`** | | Decide which hosts an agent can reach, and inject credentials without the agent ever seeing them | **`Gateway`** | | Pause an idle agent and pick up exactly where it left off | `ax suspend` / `ax resume` | | Shell into a running agent to see what it is doing | `ax ssh` | Everything is expressed as `ax.io/v1alpha1` manifests and applied with a single command. ## Quick start ### 1. Install AX ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/ax/main/install.sh | AX_VERSION=v0.4.0-rc.2 sh export PATH="$HOME/.ax/bin:$PATH" ``` > [!TIP] > Prefer a UI? Run `ax studio` to set up AX on your computer and start tasks from a local web app instead of using the CLI below. ### 2. Start AX Locally: ```bash ax local start ``` Or on an existing cluster with [Agent Substrate](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate): ```bash ax install kubectl apply -f examples/workerpool.yaml ``` To run [prebuilt agent images](https://github.com/agentexecutor/images), add the runner volume from the [release notes](https://github.com/google/ax/releases): ```bash ax local start --runner-volume-image ghcr.io/google/ax/ax-runner-volume@sha256: ``` ### Run your first task From your ax checkout: ```bash ax apply -f examples/simple.yaml # the smallest useful Task ax resume task simple-task # new tasks start Suspended; resume schedules the actor and starts it ax get tasks # NAME ATESPACE STATE ACTOR AGE # simple-task default Running simple-task 1m ax ssh simple-task -- ls -la /workspace # poke around inside the sandbox ax suspend task simple-task # checkpoint and pause ax resume task simple-task # pick up where it left off ``` The first resume also waits for the workspace to initialize (cloning its git repos), so it can take a while; if the CLI gives up first, the task keeps coming up in the background — `ax get tasks` tells you where it is. Every Task runs an image pinned by digest, named by `spec.profile.image` or `spec.profile.ateTemplate.name` or inherited from its Workspace's `spec.profile`; replace the image in `examples/simple.yaml` with `$AX_TASK_IMAGE` if you built your own. ### Prebuilt agent images Ready-to-run agent images, such as Antigravity, are published from [agentexecutor/images](https://github.com/agentexecutor/images). Each image's README has a complete Gateway and Task manifest. ### Tour Want a tour of AX end to end? Run [`./hack/tour.sh`](hack/tour.sh) against the current context. It walks through Tasks, Gateways, Workspaces with setup, suspend and resume, fan-out from a workspace snapshot, atespaces, and Models, and deletes everything it creates when it exits. ## Documentation | Guide | Read it to... | |---|---| | [Local Installer](docs/local_installer.md) | Walk through `ax local`, `ax studio`, `ax ctx`, `ax install`, and promoting tasks unchanged from local Kind to a remote GKE cluster. | | [AX Studio](https://github.com/agentexecutor/studio) | Set up AX on your computer and start, watch, and shell into tasks from a local web app (`ax studio`). | | [Concepts](docs/concepts.md) | Learn what a `Task`, `Workspace`, and `Model` each do, and how a task moves through phases and conditions. | | [Manifests](docs/manifests.md) | Write your own YAML, with an annotated example of every kind. | | [Sandbox](docs/sandbox.md) | See what the runner does on boot and what your command can rely on: metadata server, guest services, environment. | | [Runners](docs/runner.md) | Understand the contract between the control plane and the task container, and build your own runner image to replace the default. | | [Networking](docs/networking.md) | Reach a running task through the atenet router from the cluster, your laptop, or a gRPC client. | | [Observability](docs/observability.md) | Collect ax-server's logs, metrics, traces, and events, and configure where they go. | | [Architecture](DESIGN.md) | Understand how the control plane fits together, plus the [API reference](DESIGN.md#api-reference). | | [Development](docs/development.md) | Build, test, and ship changes to AX itself. | | [Roadmap](docs/roadmap.md) | See planned milestones across core specs, actor architecture, agentic environments, and governance. | ## CLI usage `ax` talks to the control plane over gRPC. It is deliberately `kubectl`-shaped: `apply`, `get`, `describe`, `delete`, plus a few agent-specific verbs. ### Everyday commands ```bash # Apply anything (multi-document YAML, file or stdin) ax apply -f examples/simple.yaml # Tasks ax get tasks # list ax get tasks -a my-atespace # list in another atespace ax get task task123 # full spec + live status as YAML ax describe task task123 # human-readable detail ax suspend task task123 # checkpoint actor state and pause ax resume task task123 # resume a suspended task ax promote task task123 --to prod # copy the task and what it binds to the cluster of kube context prod, and resume it there ax delete task task123 # Shell into the running sandbox ax ssh task123 # interactive shell (task needs spec.debug: true) ax ssh task123 -- ls -la /workspace # one-off command ax ssh task123 -- python3 main.py # Workspaces, gateways, and models follow the same pattern ax get workspaces # NAME ATESPACE GIT-REPOS MCP-SERVERS # default-workspace default 1 1 ax describe workspace default-workspace ax delete workspace default-workspace ax get gateways # NAME ATESPACE EGRESS-RULES # review-bot-gw default 3 ax describe gateway review-bot-gw ax delete gateway review-bot-gw ax get models # NAME ATESPACE PROVIDER MODEL # default-model default google gemini-3.8-flash ax describe model default-model ax delete model default-model # Environment & connection plumbing ax local start --server-image # create/resume local Kind + Substrate + AX cluster ax local status # check local environment, Substrate, and AX health ax local stop # stop local environment while keeping state ax local delete # destroy local environment and clean up owned context ax install / ax uninstall # install or remove AX on the active Kubernetes cluster ax studio # launch the AX Studio local Web UI on 127.0.0.1:8080 (needs the ax-studio binary) ax ctx # list kube contexts and active AX tunnel status ax ctx # switch active Kubernetes context in kubeconfig ax tunnel list # background tunnels (state lives in ~/.ax/tunnels) ax tunnel stop ax version ``` ### Works with `kubectx` `ax` follows your active Kubernetes context. Switch clusters and `ax` resolves and tunnels to that cluster's control plane in the background. ```bash kubectx staging-cluster ax get tasks kubectx prod-cluster ax get tasks # Or target a context without switching ax --context=dev-cluster get tasks ``` ### Global flags | Flag | Description | Default | |---|---|---| | `-a`, `--atespace` | Atespace scope for the command | `default` | | `-n`, `--namespace` | Kubernetes namespace where AX is installed | `ax-system` | | `--context` | Kubernetes context to target | active `kubectx` / `current-context` | | `--server` | Control plane address, bypassing auto-detection | derived from kube context, or `$AX_SERVER` | | `--trace` | Trace the command and print its trace ID to stderr. Its RPCs send a sampled W3C `traceparent`, and CLI spans are exported over OTLP when `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set. Without it, the CLI sends no trace context and ax-server samples on its own. See [CLI traces](docs/observability.md#cli-traces) | off | ## AX and Agent Substrate [Agent Substrate](https://github.com/agent-substrate/substrate) is the compute runtime layer AX relies on. It schedules actors onto workers, isolates them, and suspends, resumes and snapshots them. It also handles their networking, egress policies and credential injection. Agent Substrate is a low-opinion system in terms of agentic abstractions. Besides task execution, AX and Agent Substrate are orthogonal to each other. AX is aiming to grow into an agentic platform that covers session management, memory, multi-task coordination, input steering, registries, models, and trajectory collection. We are building it at Google as our portable agentic platform, one that runs the same way inside Google, on customer clusters, and on-prem. ## License Apache License 2.0.
